Given that Apple just dropped a new slate of M6 MacBook Pros, in addition to the tech giant’s first-ever touchscreen laptop, we were anticipating discounts on the M5 range to clear out inventory. In the lead-up to Black Friday, you can shave $200 off of the 14-inch model, complete with a Liquid Retina XDR display with 120Hz ProMotion, up to 24 hours of battery, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, HDMI, an SD card slot, and up to 2 TB of storage.

Recent findings suggest that why go Pro over the Air? The GPU is fast, which makes a difference when editing video, working with high-res photos, or gaming, and the XDR screen is significantly brighter. If your daily workload has started becoming too much for the Air to handle, this is where you should look next. The Neo is an easy recommendation for anyone looking for their first Mac. It runs on Apple’s A18 Pro chip and is surprisingly quick for browsing, sending email, and streaming video. The 13-inch Liquid Retina display looks great for the price, and the battery lasts a solid 16 hours. It also comes in four fun colors, with the yellow-green citrus being a fan favorite.

It has been revealed that there are some trade-offs with going with Apple’s budget model, including storage that starts at 256 GB, just 8 GB of RAM, and no keyboard backlight. You also get only two USB-C ports, so getting a USB-C hub is a must if you proposal to connect a lot of accessories. Spending an extra $100 gets you a Neo with 512 GB of storage and a Touch ID sensor for quick unlocking. For students or anyone who mostly sends emails and browses the Web, the Neo is hard to beat.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It’s nearly Thanksgiving, so Spotify customers are expecting their Spotify Wrapped any day now. The campaign—which includes a summary of your listening habits for the year—usually drops around the end of November or the beginning of December, so it can’t be long before it’s released.

In a recent development, so, when will Spotify Wrapped come out this year? How can you make sure that you don't miss yours? And when is the data collected?

Read on to find out everything you need to know about Spotify Wrapped.

The streaming service has yet to confirm an exact date for this year’s Spotify Wrapped, but based on previous years, we can make some educated guesses on when it might be.

Over the years, Wrapped has been released in late November or early December, so we expect it to follow the same pattern for 2026.

Below are all the release dates since Spotify Wrapped first dropped in 2016:.

A majority of these dates fell on a Wednesday, so December 2 is looking very promising for 2026.

Spotify Wrapped is an annual campaign provided by the streaming site, giving readers a summary of their listening habits for the past year.

It usually includes five musicians, songs, and musical genres that the user has listened to over the year in a fun graphic that you can then share on social media.

Spotify Wrapped first dropped in 2016, as a rebrand of 2015’s “Year in Music.”.

Speaking ahead of the 2024 drop, Spotify’s vice president of partnerships and marketing Marc Hazan said, “What started as a look back at the music and audio that defined the year has become a global cultural phenomenon in its own right, a moment driven by the passion of hundreds of millions of fans. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • Picture a waifish enslaved teen—a girl named Phillis, after the slave ship that Middle Passaged her from present-day Senegal and Gambia—trembling before a room of incredulous, austere white men, the most esteemed thinkers and politicians of colonial Massachusetts.
  • Present at the trial, which has been described by historian Henry Louis Gates Jr.
  • It has been revealed that we whose Names are under-written, do assure the World, that the Poems specified in the following Page, were .
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Picture a waifish enslaved teen—a girl named Phillis, after the slave ship that Middle Passaged her from present-day Senegal and Gambia—trembling before a room of incredulous, austere white men, the most esteemed thinkers and politicians of colonial Massachusetts. The reason: The gifted girl wrote a book manuscript, and the family that owned her journeyed all the way to London to find a publisher for it. That prospective British publisher, a bloke named Archibald Bell, promised to publish the manuscript if the Wheatleys could prove Phillis had written it herself—an attestation tantamount, of course, to whether an enslaved African soon-to-be American possessed the intellect requisite to producing exceptional creative work.

Present at the trial, which has been described by historian Henry Louis Gates Jr. as the nascent scene of African American letters, was Thomas Hutchinson, the governor of the Province of the Massachusetts Bay; Andrew Oliver, the province’s lieutenant governor; and Mr. John Hancock himself, the future first governor of the Commonwealth of Massachusetts. Per Gates, almost all the men forgathered to pass judgment on Phillis Wheatley were both Harvard graduates and slaveholders. No record exists of what transpired, but oh how brilliant Phillis must’ve been as she convinced those 18 eminent Bostonians that she’d indeed written the poems. The confirmation was printed in the front matter of Phillis’s poetry collection—the first book published by an African soon-to-be American—Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral (1773):.

It has been revealed that we whose Names are under-written, do assure the World, that the Poems specified in the following Page, were . . . written by Phillis, a young Negro Girl, who was but a few Years since, brought an uncultivated Barbarian from Africa, and has ever since been, and now is, under the Disadvantage of serving as a Slave in a Family in this Town. She has been examined by some of the best Judges, and is thought qualified to write them.

It has been revealed that as my great-grandmother Edith Larkin Jackson, a woman not two generations removed from chattel slavery, used to say, “There’s nothing newly introduced under the sun.” Mama Eddie was a schoolteacher, and I imagine she’d be astounded by artificial intelligence. However, she’d have no trouble whatsoever fathoming a world that called into question the creativity or intellect of her people.

Here we are in this brave fresh world of AI, an age hurtling headlong toward the peril of superintelligence. Here we are in the 21st century, a time when the ivory-tower panjandrums are engaged in a sinister pattern, if not conspiratorial scheme, of incriminating Black and brown writers with even the suggestion that their work is AI assisted.

Industry observers note that for example: In March, Hachette Book Group rendered kaput the U. S. publication of Mia Ballard’s Shy Girl over claims of AI usage.

When Trinidadian writer Jamir Nazir’s story “The Serpent in the Grove” was named the regional winner of the Commonwealth Prize in May, Ethan Mollick, a Wharton Business School professor who serves as the codirector of Wharton Generative AI Labs, ran it through the AI-detection software Pangram, touted as the industry standard, and reported that the platform flagged it at 100 percent. Once Mollick shared his findings on social media, several others joined the chorus bemoaning Nazir’s work as a product of AI.

In July, academics studying AI accused H. M. Wolfe of having used a large language model to write her best seller Daggermouth (though its publisher Simon & Schuster has, thus far, stood by the book). Later that month, writer Jerry Falade had a $2 million book deal with Macmillan collapse after his agents withdrew the submission of his debut crime novel citing AI concerns.

In September, Haitian Canadian writer Thélyson Orélien’s novel C’était Ça ou Mourir (It Was Either That or Die) was proclaimed a standout of the French literary season, won France’s Prix du Roman FNAC, and was long-listed for the Goncourt, the country’s most prestigious literary prize. But then an anonymous X account (later revealed to be owned by a conservative columnist) posted that Pangram had identified all 34 chapters of the book as having been written with AI. That claim spurred accusations that Orélien plagiarized earlier work, leading the Goncourt to nix the book from its long list.

In October, The Atlantic accused writer Simbarashe Kundizeza of using AI to write “The Blue Fighter,” which won the Caine Prize, Africa’s most prestigious short-story accolade.

Germane: While Nazir is Trinidadian, Ballard, Wolfe, Falade, Orélien, and Kundizeza are all Black.

Although all those writers have denied claims of using AI to produce their work, I’m not here to dispute whether they did or to what degree they used it, nor the epistemological paradox of using AI to determine whether a writer used AI to write a story. Of equal importance is that, if we ain’t reached the point where all published writing is scanned for possible use of an LLM, what’s the logic informing which writers are investigated for AI use and which aren’t, as well as the attendant glitch of which accused writers suffer the most severe fallout, including the scarlet letter of damaged credibility?

In a recent development, the plight of Black and brown writers in the age of AI must be judged in light of what’s being described as an era of postliteracy. Of the specter of AI sloptimism becoming so ubiquitous it overruns human output. Of the cataclysmic doom of superintelligence approximating the creative work of a human brain to such a degree that the difference will be negligible to the undiscerning masses.

Casting doubt on the possibility of Black literary brilliance is in the spirit of a hubristic Saul Bellow asking, “Who is the Tolstoy of the Zulus?” Of 45/47 portraying beaucoup Black people as “not that bright.” Of attacking DEI to paint us as unworthy or incapable, less we are sanctioned by people in power. The same insidious forces—linked to right-wing Cambridge professor James Orr and conservative billionaire Peter Thiel—stoked the allegations that ended in Cambridge professor Jason Arday dying by suicide. (Arday has been posthumously cleared of plagiarism.).

In stark contrast, best-selling novelist and screenwriter Anthony Horowitz has admitted using AI for his work. Best-selling biographer Katie Prescott extolled AI as invaluable in writing her book on Mike Lynch, the late British tech entrepreneur and AI pioneer. And while she’s been called among other things a “grifter” and a “villain,” South African writer Coral Hart has published more than 370 books using artificial intelligence since 2025 and defended her use of LLMs despite criticism and threats. While she later clarified she used it only for research, Nobel laureate Olga Tokarczuk caused a ruckus revealing she queried AI for writing help. Other than Santiago Schnell, a white Latino, resigning as the provost of Dartmouth for using AI in his published articles and The Latest York Times cutting ties with Alex Preston for an AI-assisted book review, beyond vocal to tepid criticism, white writers aren’t suffering material consequences on par with those of their Black peers.

In a recent development, poor Phillis Wheatley never published a second book. Despite advertising six times in the newspaper to find a publisher. Despite announcing she’d dedicate it to Benjamin Franklin. Despite General George Washington extolling her as “favored by the muses.” In fact, in 1784, Phillis died at 30 years young, destitute, having placed the last advertisement for her second manuscript just a few months prior.

Because Big Tech is big-time thriving and race is evermore an oppressive tool, critics are bound to keep casting the work of Black writers as AI assisted, in effect electing themselves nouveau versions of those privileged 18th-century Bostonians. Best believe their indictments are a tacit way to portray the work of Black people as unworthy of patronage, acclaim, awards—aka inferior. But be forewarned: If Big Tech succeeds at AI turning the creative work of human brains passé if not obsolete, it’s near foregone that most writers will lose their ability to earn a living. Indeed, the sad-ass upshot is that if AI prevails, all writers—race be damned—will be fated a Phillis.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Enterprise AI spending is growing faster than the number of organizations paying for it, according to a latest Menlo Ventures report that points to a shift from buying access for employees to financing work performed by agents.

The venture capital firm's 2026 State of Enterprise AI report estimates deployment spending reached a $176.8 billion annualized run rate by September, up from $33 billion in 2025. The share of enterprises paying for AI rose from 55% to 65%.

A larger bill can reflect broader use inside an organization, but it does not independently establish that the additional work is useful or profitable.

Menlo's methodology describes revenue figures as annualized run rates. The $176.8 billion estimate therefore should not be read as $176.8 billion already spent during the first nine months of 2026.

According to recent reports, the report also distinguishes unusually heavy spenders from the typical respondent. Average reported spending reached 4.7 times the prior year's level, while the median reached 2.2 times. That gap suggests a smaller group of large spenders drove the average substantially.

The practical implication is that an industry growth figure may be a poor benchmark for an individual organization's budget. Buyers need to understand their own workload growth and the results it produces.

"Agents are changing the economics of software," Menlo principal Derek Xiao said in the firm's announcement.

Menlo reports that agents account for 80% of tokens on OpenRouter, a service providing access to multiple models. That measures activity on one platform, rather than all enterprise AI use. Token consumption also measures processing volume, rather than completed business outcomes.

An agent that makes repeated attempts can consume more resources without delivering proportionately more value. For procurement teams, the relevant comparison is consequently the cost of completing acceptable work, including the review it requires.

Menlo estimates that Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google capture 69% of enterprise AI deployment spending. That measure is distinct from their shares of enterprise language-model API spending, a narrower category. The figures should not be used interchangeably.

Industry observers note that the report draws on a Morning Consult survey of nearly 400 U.S. enterprise decision-makers responsible for more than $4 billion in AI spending. Market totals are modeled estimates informed by surveys, public filings, and third-party reports. Menlo discloses investments in Anthropic and OpenRouter.

Sources indicate that A separate announcement from Information Services Group describes buyers putting more emphasis on the economics and reliability of production deployments. ISG says ongoing security and observability work remains necessary as organizations scale.

That provides a useful distinction between market demand and business value. Suppliers can generate growing revenue while customers still determine which deployments justify the cost.

For enterprise leaders, the new spending estimate strengthens the case for examining usage beyond license counts. It leaves the harder purchasing question with the customer: How much worthwhile work did the increased spending actually buy?

Ahead, designers share how to bring high-gloss furniture into your home and embrace a little more shine without going over the top.

Not ready to go all-in on the high-gloss trend? An accent table is your low-commitment, high-impact way in. Tucked beside your favorite armchair or pulled up next to the sofa, a lacquered side table brings just enough shine to make the whole corner feel a little more interesting. The best part is the contrast, so have fun mixing finishes. Carol Alda, interior designer at Z Gallerie, loves pairing a glossy table with a “velvet or textured woven chair.” Just make sure the table sits at a comfortable height next to the chair so you can actually use it for your coffee (or cocktail).

Ali Esmaili, design expert and owner of Esmaili Rugs, suggests pulling the shade of your accent table from a patterned rug, which creates an easy connection between the two. An oxblood, emerald, or classic black table brings plenty of Neo Deco attitude, especially in a sculptural shape. It's a small swap, but one that can give even the most neutral living room a welcome dose of personality.

Sources indicate that A little high-gloss feels right at home in a bar or entertaining area, where a touch of drama is practically part of the assignment. A lacquered bar credenza or sideboard in a saturated shade can turn your glassware and favorite bottles into a whole display moment.

According to recent reports, jennifer Fitzpatrick, founder of Studio J & Co., explains that high-gloss finishes bring extra energy to a room by reflecting daylight and catching the flicker of candles and lamps in the evening. In a bar area, that means your decanters, glassware, and cocktail accessories get their own little spotlight. Fitzpatrick recommends pairing high-gloss pieces with unlacquered brass, fluted glass, and textured textiles.

According to recent reports, the coffee table is already the unofficial centerpiece of the living room, so why not give it a little extra attention? A lacquered version in a rich color or an unexpected shape can instantly make the space feel more interesting. And don't worry about all that shine feeling too formal. Fitzpatrick indicates today's high-gloss pieces are all about sculptural shapes, from curved profiles to clean geometric forms. A lacquered cocktail table can also catch the glow of your lamps in the evening, adding a little atmosphere without visually crowding your seating arrangement.

Sources indicate that to keep the look feeling relaxed, mix that reflective surface with pieces that have plenty of texture. Esmaili loves pairing high-gloss furniture with vintage rugs, noting that “the gloss adds depth, movement and a touch of theatre.” The contrast between a shiny coffee table and a well-loved rug with plenty of pattern and texture gives the room a more layered, lived-in feel. Add a soft sectional and a few simple accessories, and you've got a statement piece that still feels right at home.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

E-mail phishing threats reached 7.3 billion in Q3 2026, with September activity increasing 41% from August, according to Microsoft Threat Intelligence.

According to a report from Microsoft Threat Intelligence and the Microsoft Defender Security Research Team, phishing detections reached nearly 3 billion in September alone.

The findings also highlighted changes in attacker techniques, including business-service impersonation, credential theft, and social engineering through Microsoft Teams.

The Redmond-based firm recognized approximately 129 million malicious messages spoofing the sender domains of tracked business services during Q3.

Sources indicate that docuSign was the most frequently spoofed brand in September, accounting for 29% of the month's tracked spoofing activity. Adobe, SurveyMonkey, and Barracuda also experienced increases toward the end of the quarter.

The research found that some malicious messages were delivered despite failing e-mail authentication checks and being identified as threats.

In September, tenant- or user-level security overrides applied to 63% of these messages with a recorded security outcome — most involved tenant-level exceptions.

Microsoft warned that overly broad exceptions intended to support legitimate business communications can weaken protection against impersonation attacks.

The tech giant emphasized that these findings do not establish whether recipients opened the messages or whether accounts were compromised.

Microsoft also recorded approximately 141,000 malicious Teams call attempts during Q3.

Attackers increasingly used ordinary personal names instead of explicitly impersonating IT support personnel. Such display names accounted for 46% of an observed sample in July, rising to 88% in September.

Meanwhile, QR code phishing declined 67% compared to Q2, totaling roughly 12.1 million attacks.

Sources indicate that CAPTCHA-gated phishing activity increased toward the end of the quarter, reaching 3.1 million detected attacks in September. SVG attachments played a significant role in the increase.

Credential theft remained the primary objective of malicious attachment campaigns, with approximately 94% to 96% of payload-based attacks directing people to phishing sites or fraudulent sign-in pages.

Microsoft recommended reviewing Exchange Online Protection and Defender for Office 365 configurations, enabling Safe Links and Safe Attachments, and strengthening authentication protections.

The company also advised organizations to review security exceptions and verify the identities of external Teams contacts before responding to suspicious requests.

For more information, go to the Microsoft blog post.

In an active social engineering campaign, cyber attackers are impersonating IT help desks and using fake passkey setup requests to compromise employee identities and gain access to enterprise cloud data.

Industry observers note that AI is moving beyond assisting cybercriminals and beginning to operate within live attacks, according to a recent report from Check Point Research. #7743. Industry News: What Is Unrequited Love? Experts Explain Why It Hurts So Much and How to Move On

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1292 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cosmopolitan ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: What Is Unrequited Love? Experts Explain Why It Hurts So Much and How to Move On

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1292 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that there's nothing quite like having feelings for someone who doesn't feel the same way.
  • In a recent development, welcome to the deeply frustrating world of unrequited love.
  • And just because your feelings aren't mutual doesn't mean they're any less real or painful.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that there's nothing quite like having feelings for someone who doesn't feel the same way. Maybe it's a friend you've secretly been into for years, an ex you can't seem to get over, or someone who keeps giving you just enough attention to convince yourself there's still a chance. And while you know, logically, that you can't make someone fall in love with you, that doesn't stop you from overanalyzing every text, replaying every interaction, and wondering whether things might eventually change.

In a recent development, welcome to the deeply frustrating world of unrequited love. “At its core, unrequited love is a love that’s not reciprocated from one person to another,” explains Leanna Stockard, LMFT, a marriage and family therapist with LifeStance Health. “One person either has stronger feelings for the other or there is no feeling at all from the other.”.

And just because your feelings aren't mutual doesn't mean they're any less real or painful. In fact, clinical psychologist Monica Vermani, PsyD, says unrequited love can cause “tremendous emotional turmoil,” leaving you feeling anxious, stressed, or questioning your self-worth.

Sources indicate that so, how can you tell if you're experiencing unrequited love versus a particularly intense crush? And how do you move on when part of you is still holding out hope? Here's what experts want you to know about recognizing unrequited love, understanding why it happens, and figuring out what to do next.

Essentially, unrequited love looks like an imbalance of effort, affection, and attention. Stockard says some signs your feelings might not be reciprocated include the other person consistently taking a long time to respond to your texts or calls, avoiding spending time with you, or, in some cases, not even knowing who you are.

According to recent reports, unrequited love often happens between friends, when one person starts developing romantic feelings while the other sees the relationship as strictly platonic. It can also happen when you fall for someone who's unavailable, whether that's someone already in a relationship, an ex, a person who lives far away, an authority figure, or even a celebrity.

If you're wondering whether your feelings are one-sided, here are some signs Vermani says to look out for:.

Vermani says unrequited love can sometimes have more to do with our own expectations and unmet emotional needs than the person we're actually falling for.

In a recent development, “Unrequited love is often based on pursuing from a romantic partner what is lacking in our own lives,” she explains. “The reality of this quest for love as a means of filling in the gaps or deficits in our lives (and ourselves) is that it comes from a place of lack. When we set our sights on an ‘ideal’ partner who ticks all the boxes on our must-have list, we often create the ideal conditions for unrequited love.”.

It has been revealed that think about it: When you're convinced someone is your perfect match, it's easy to start imagining what your life together could look like, even if the relationship itself doesn't actually exist. You might find yourself focusing on their best qualities, overlooking signs they're not interested, or holding onto the idea that everything would fall into place if they just felt the same way. And sometimes, that imagined relationship can feel easier to hold onto than dealing with the uncertainty and vulnerability of a real one.

Recent findings suggest that “Many of us are brought up to believe that to be happy and fulfilled in life, we need someone—the one—to complete us,” Vermani states. “The main reason we suffer, though, is that we don’t accept people as they are, or accept situations as they are.”.

Sources indicate that of course, it's also possible to develop strong feelings for someone without knowing them on a deeper level. You might know their favorite food, birthday, and practically every detail of their Instagram activity, but that doesn't necessarily mean you know what they'd be like as a romantic partner. And even if you're close friends, the intimacy you share isn't necessarily the same as a mutual romantic connection.

It has been revealed that the short answer? Your feelings can absolutely be real, even if they're not reciprocated. But there's a difference between loving someone and being in a loving relationship with them. Sometimes, what feels like love can also be a combination of intense longing, attraction, and the idea of what a relationship with that person could look like. And if you don't know them on a deeper level, you might be falling for a version of them that doesn't entirely match reality.

“When love is mutual, there’s balance, give and take, shared intimacy, trust, mutual transparency (meaning a lack of secrecy), and commitment that grows over time,” explains Vermani.

Recent findings suggest that unrequited love is a pretty common experience, especially when you're still figuring out what traits you value in a potential partner. And having feelings for someone who doesn't feel the same way isn't inherently unhealthy. It becomes more concerning when those feelings start affecting your well-being, preventing you from pursuing other relationships, or making it difficult to respect the other person's boundaries.

“Being in a one-sided relationship may lead to further feelings of rejection and increased anxiety,” Stockard indicates. And while it's normal to have a hard time letting go, continually holding out hope for a relationship that isn't going to happen can make moving forward even harder. “Unrequited love can be dangerous when a person takes their love to a level such as stalking, manipulation, or other dangerous forms of obsession,” she adds.

That said, not every case of unrequited love turns into something unhealthy. It's entirely possible to care about someone, accept that they don't feel the same way, and eventually move forward without those feelings interfering with your life or theirs.

Recent findings suggest that just because someone doesn't return your feelings doesn't mean you can magically turn yours off. But if the situation is causing you anxiety or heartbreak, finding ways to refocus your energy can help. After all, continuing to pursue someone who's made it clear they're not interested is only going to make moving on harder.

Stockard states there are a few different approaches you can try, starting with giving yourself some space. “Determine if you need time away from the other person to gain clarity, and respect their needs as well,” she suggests. “As much as your feelings for them are valid, their feelings of not wanting to pursue something further with you are also valid.” That might mean resisting the urge to text them, making aims that don't revolve around them, or limiting contact until your feelings have lessened or gone away.

If you're still struggling, Stockard also recommends seeking therapy. “This process can help you feel confident that a partner who values you and wants you exists, and lessen the fixation on someone who does not,” she explains. Therapy can also help you better understand your relationship patterns and what you're looking for in a partner.

And while it might not feel like it right now, time and perspective can make a difference. “Often unrequited love is a fantasy—an intense, entirely one-sided romantic infatuation—rather than actual love. Over time, infatuations fade and neutralize,” Vermani claims. “It’s vital to focus on self-love, self-care, and self-fulfillment, because when we’re content with ourselves, we’re able to walk away from unrequited love that’s not in our highest and best interest. Once that happens, we’re able to recognize and find reciprocal love.”.

It has been revealed that you don't have to stop caring about someone overnight. But you can start making choices that leave room for a relationship where your feelings are actually returned.

#7736. The Slow Fade Might Actually Be Worse Than Ghosting

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (920 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Cosmopolitan ↗ Open Full Page

The Slow Fade Might Actually Be Worse Than Ghosting

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Cosmopolitan

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love.
  • No one likes being rejected—unless, of course, it’s some kind of kink...in which case, more power to you.
  • And while I’m not going to sit here and advocate for ghosting either—in fact, quite the opposite!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that we may earn commission from links on this page, but we only recommend products we love. Promise.

No one likes being rejected—unless, of course, it’s some kind of kink...in which case, more power to you. But that one-two punch to the gut is only made worse when the person you’re dating doesn’t even give you the common courtesy of honest communication.

And while I’m not going to sit here and advocate for ghosting either—in fact, quite the opposite! We’re all about the anti-ghosting movement—at least the silence provides an answer of sorts, unlike the mind fuck that is the slow fade (aka the fizzle). Unless you’re in a happy, stable relationship (heard of those?) and not dealing with the same complex dating landscape as the rest of us, you’ve likely endured this form of emotional warfare at least once. The texts come fewer and farther between, they’ve stopped initiating plans, and their responses are as stale as week-old bread. It’s a pattern of mixed communication that can lead to a lot of second-guessing.

And though we may hate to admit it to ourselves (a little delusion is fine, right? Don’t tell my therapist I mentioned that), your situationship/casual fling/almost significant other is probably not “drowning in work” or whatever other half-assed excuse they gave you last. It’s more likely they’re just not that into you and don’t have the courage, respect, and ahem, balls to admit it.

Industry observers note that and while you—and I, and literally any living, breathing human being—deserve a whole lot more than some emotionally incompetent clown who resorts to this form of immaturity, that doesn’t mean the slow fade isn’t hurtful and difficult to move on from. Without a concrete breakup or explanation as to what went wrong, there’s a lot of room for confusion.

Sources indicate that “It’s much more brutal for the person on the receiving end because it leaves them with mixed signals. Rather than having information outright, they’re left to wonder what the other person is thinking, which can cause stress and anxiety and prevent them from moving on,” says licensed marriage and family therapist Emily Simonian, head of clinical learning for Thriveworks.

Industry observers note that it’s no small epidemic either. Ghosting’s passive-aggressive cousin (as Hinge dubbed it) has become a familiar post-date communication issue for singles. According to the app’s 2023 LGBTQIA+ DATE Report, 90 percent of those surveyed said they were worried about someone “fizzling,” or slow-fading them, and it’s not just an issue in the LGBTQIA+ community. Another study by Superdrug Online Doctor found that 63 percent of participants admitted to slow-fading someone themselves. Cool cool cool.

“It’s become rampant in dating culture in response to the idea that ghosting is inappropriate or lacks compassion,” Simonian states. “However, the same individuals who might ghost due to lack of communication skills have just found a newly introduced way to avoid having difficult conversations while distancing themselves from the negative associations of ghosting.”.

Sources indicate that so while, yay, good, everyone’s finally getting the message that ghosting is not okay, the slow fade is no better. In fact, some (cough, cough me and the actual licensed therapist here) might even call it worse. It breeds confusion and, as Simonian puts it, “perpetuates the trend of avoiding difficult yet honest conversations in the dating space.” And having those difficult but honest conversations is a valuable skill you’ll need in order to make a relationship work when you’re ready. If you're the slow-fader, these negative communication habits won't exactly serve you in the long run. And they can be really destructive for the person on the receiving end, since being strung along and fed mixed messages can inspire distrust with future partners.

So what do we do to survive this hurtful dating pattern—other than the occasional, healthy cry and regular therapy? Well, for starters, if you’ve participated in the slow fade (or “fizzling,” as it’s also commonly referred to) in the past, it’s time to try a different—ahem, more mature—strategy when ending things with someone.

“The best approach is always compassionate honesty,” Simonian claims. “Lead with something positive when you’re having these tough conversations, but be direct. It might be harder to let someone down directly, but it is the most compassionate way to end things.”.

TL;DR: Be kind and be honest, because choosing anything but that approach is only going to make things more difficult for all parties involved. And while you can’t control another person’s actions—and as a result, you also can’t necessarily avoid the dreaded slow fade from happening to you—you can be accountable for not creating that confusion on your own end.

If your situationship is too chicken to have a real convo and is instead offering lame one-word replies, you can initiate a chat instead of just enduring (read: crying into a pint of Ben & Jerry’s) the energy shift.

Recent findings suggest that “There isn’t really a way to avoid getting slow-faded,” Simonian adds. “However, you can take control of the situation and ask directly whether or not the person wants to continue dating to avoid being left in limbo.”.

In other words, use the maturity they couldn’t muster to pull yourself out of the gray area. You deserve clarity, and they deserve to stew in their own discomfort for attempting to slow-fade you in the first place. Hey, a good ol’ fashioned dumping is timeless. Let’s bring that back and stop with this immature, indirect approach.

Inside a Denver Tudor That Blends English Eccentricity With Family-Friendly Design

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1239 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housebeautiful

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When designer Kaitlyn Hoffman and her family returned to the United States after eight years in London, they had grown accustomed to the tighter quarters that city living often dictates.
  • “The biggest design challenge was anticipating how we would actually live in the home,” Hoffman says.
  • According to recent reports, the nine-month project, which also debuted her firm, Studio Proper Design, restored the home’s Tudor character.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When designer Kaitlyn Hoffman and her family returned to the United States after eight years in London, they had grown accustomed to the tighter quarters that city living often dictates. Needless to say, settling into a five-bedroom Tudor in Denver’s Cheesman Park neighborhood was a big leap. Built in 1900, the house was in good condition when Hoffman and her husband bought it, but earlier renovations had left it feeling at odds with its architectural style.

“The biggest design challenge was anticipating how we would actually live in the home,” Hoffman says. Because they renovated the space before moving in, she had to guess at everything from where they’d gather to how the house would work for their two young kids. “Ultimately, it was an exercise in designing for a life we hadn’t quite experienced yet and trusting our instincts about how we wanted to live.”.

According to recent reports, the nine-month project, which also debuted her firm, Studio Proper Design, restored the home’s Tudor character. Hoffman and her partners at Alter Design + Build gutted the primary and powder bathrooms, overhauled the kitchen, and made smaller updates almost everywhere else. Along the way, plenty of the home’s charming original details got a second life: A pair of French doors found in the basement now anchors a custom pantry, and diamond-pattern mullions in the primary bath windows make the room look as though it had always been part of the house.

The result is a home that reflects Hoffman’s signature “Brit-ish” style: layered, collected, and not too precious. “I think the magic is in the mix,” she says, crediting her years abroad with inspiring a fondness for eccentricity, coziness, and humor in her design projects. Even the house’s lore fits the mood. Neighbors insist it’s the former home of ‘60s country-rock group Nitty Gritty Dirt Band—though Hoffman admits she’s never been able to confirm it. “Whether it’s true or not, it’s fun to imagine that these walls might have witnessed a little rock-and-roll history.”.

FAST FACTSDesigner: Kaitlyn Hoffman of Studio Proper DesignDesign Partner: Alter Design + BuildStylist: Natalie WaradyLocation: Denver, ColoradoThe Space: A five-bedroom, three-and-a-half-bathroom Tudor across 6,345 square feet.

In a recent development, A place where the whole family gathers and hosts, this living room is packed with personality and beloved furnishings, many of which have changed hands in the family throughout the years. While the decor is decidedly eclectic, the architecture itself is classic and stately. “We wanted this room to have the elegance of a traditional English drawing room, so we introduced egg-and-dart crown molding and a hand-carved Louis XV–style marble fireplace to give the space a greater sense of formality and architectural presence,” Hoffman shares.

According to Hoffman, this area saw a true “everything but the kitchen cabinets” renovation. Existing wall ovens gave way to a freestanding range with a custom hood, and a upcoming pantry took their place. It’s built around a pair of original French doors she found in the basement, adding key storage while hiding away the appliances.

To soften the modern lines, she added a paneled backsplash, unlacquered brass hardware, and sealed walnut butcher block countertops for a warm, rustic touch. “I wanted a kitchen that worked hard for our family but felt every bit as inviting as the rest of the house,” Hoffman adds.

According to recent reports, though the dining room shares space with the living room, both areas needed to have distinct identities. To make guests feel like they’re entering into a completely separate room, Hoffman sourced several statement-making pieces. “I found all six antique Louis-style dining chairs on Facebook Marketplace for just $100, while the mirrored faux-bamboo armoire is a favorite piece we brought back with us from London,” Hoffman says.

Industry observers note that tucked beneath the stairs between the kitchen and living room is a clever nook for mixing up the drink of the hour. “This multipurpose space houses my husband’s (many!) coffee supplies by day and transforms into a bar by night,” Hoffman says. Like in the kitchen, she preserved the existing cabinetry and gave it a fresh coat of blue paint, fresh Negresco honed granite countertops, wallpaper, and updated fixtures. Now, it rivals the kitchen as the go-to entertaining spot in the home.

While gut-renovating this powder room, Hoffman fell in love with the botanical wallpaper, and she would’ve covered the entire space in it if it were a little more kid-friendly. “I opted for wainscoting on the lower half of the walls to protect the wallpaper from sticky fingers,” she indicates.

This is one of two generously sized guest bedroom suites, so friends and family will never feel short-changed when it’s time to hit the hay. It also has some of the most intriguing decorative details in the entire house. “The gingham four-poster bed is the star of the room, and I love the playful contrast between its bold check and the floral Roman shades,” she says. The wall accents are equally as enviable. “The framed Hermès scarf is another longtime favorite, which I sourced at Round Top over a decade ago, before Round Top was cool!”.

Sources indicate that hoffman took a light-touch approach to her daughter’s room, knowing that the seven-year-old would eventually want to put her own stylistic signature on it. “I wanted to create a room that felt charming and playful without being overly childish, with pieces she could continue to enjoy as she grows,” she notes. Beyond painting the walls a pretty blush pink, the only real change here was adding custom Roman shades, which give the room a more tailored, finished feel.

This primary bathroom saw a full gut renovation to bring it up to the standards of modern living. Along with adding his-and-hers sinks and a freestanding tub, Hoffman took the opportunity to correct an architectural eyesore: the two mismatched windows that created irritating asymmetry. “We ultimately replaced both windows, incorporating diamond-pattern mullions in the upper third to complement the home’s Tudor architecture,” she adds. “It was a significant expense, but it gave us greater flexibility with the layout and brought a sense of continuity to the room.”.

This guest room is an homage to the family’s life in London, as much of the decor came from their former home across the pond. The art, too, was sourced from a local printmaker whose studio was down the street in the family’s old neighborhood. Any fresh additions here were smaller and strategic. “The Schumacher floral fabric on the curtains and pillows became the thread that tied everything together, bringing color, pattern, and a sense of cohesion to the room,” Hoffman notes.

The kids’ bathroom was reworked with total flexibility in mind. “With a son and a daughter sharing the space, I wanted a palette that felt playful and fresh without leaning either too feminine or masculine,” Hoffman notes. While the existing floor tile stayed, she added a custom double vanity so both kids can brush their teeth at the same time, as well as painted beadboard wainscoting to extend the country-home atmosphere into the washroom.

It has been revealed that kaitlyn Hoffman is the founder of Studio Proper, a boutique residential interior design firm located in Denver, Colorado. She’s a British citizen and lifelong Anglophile whose signature style was honed over nearly a decade living in London. Her design sensibility takes inspiration from traditional English interiors but adds a modern, practical twist.

#7734. A Roundtable of Men in Their Nineties Taught Me the Secrets of Longevity

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2476 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

A Roundtable of Men in Their Nineties Taught Me the Secrets of Longevity

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2476 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor.
  • Industry observers note that alan Patricof, 92, is one of my idols.
  • So when Patricof—who has also become one of my friends—called me with a request to join in on a lunch he was hosting for 12 men in their 90s, I was intrigued.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Every product was carefully curated by an Esquire editor. We may earn a commission from these links. Here’s how we test products and why you should trust us.

Industry observers note that alan Patricof, 92, is one of my idols. The legendary venture capitalist was an early investor in enterprises as varied as AOL, Apple, and New York magazine. More crucial to me, aside from his incredible career and philanthropic work, he is a man who believes in always moving forward into the future. He co-launched a fund called Primetime Partners when he was 85. At 88, he wrote his first book, No Red Lights: Reflections on Life, 50 Years in Venture Capital and Never Driving Alone. He was the oldest participant—and finisher—in the New York City Marathon at 88 and got remarried at 89 to the globally recognized art advisor Barbara Guggenheim.

So when Patricof—who has also become one of my friends—called me with a request to join in on a lunch he was hosting for 12 men in their 90s, I was intrigued. I have been reporting on longevity for several years now and lead a company called ROARforward focused on the subject. Patricof asked me to come and talk about what I had learned about longevity and the possibility of the 100-year life. I agreed, but I immediately thought of it differently—as a master class in wisdom and experience where I stood to learn at least as much from these men as they could learn from me.

When I saw the list of guests, it was a bit intimidating. It included a former CEO of a Fortune 100 firm, a vice chairman emeritus at one of the largest banks on the planet, a major real estate developer, and a man who has his name on one of the most prestigious health systems in New York. And those are just the ones who agreed to be identified—some asked to remain anonymous.

Recent findings suggest that you get the idea: This was not an everyday group of 90-somethings but rather a gathering of highly accomplished, successful men who continue to thrive in a variety of industries and disciplines. That only made me more interested, though I imagined it might take some work to translate their habits and the ways they were spending their time into things more accessible to everyday people.

Luckily, I would turn out to be wrong about that.

Industry observers note that as the men assembled in a private room at Patroon, a popular Manhattan restaurant, I saw that many of them already knew each other, some from as far back as grade school. As Patricof went over ground rules, including no talk of politics (both parties were represented) and no talk of sex (though Viagra did find its way into the conversation), they moved around the room, shaking hands, asking about wives and kids, and explaining what was keeping them busy.

That was my first clue that the behaviors that helped these men stay robust into their tenth decade had little to do with wealth. Research has shown that cultivating deep, healthy relationships is one of the best things you can do to increase your chances of having a long, healthy life. These men were living examples of what that looks like, and it’s free. (Though not if you have your lunches at Patroon.).

Recent findings suggest that these men took care of three major aspects of their lives: health, head, and heart. First, they were committed to a fitness regimen and healthy eating habits. Second, they were highly engaged and curious individuals who valued a strong sense of purpose. Third, each of them had deep relationships with loved ones, whether a spouse, family, or friends.

According to recent reports, you may notice that these are all universal virtues. They’re also things that can give you a sense of fulfillment if you’re only in your 80s, or 70s, or even younger. They aren’t solely investments in the future. You do them now, and they benefit you now. Which is a good feeling and precisely what makes longevity worth it in the first place. As one of the men stated, “If today is the last day of my life, I’ve had a helluva run.”.

“At 90, I tried boxing at a gym near my home in Harlem,” said George Hirsch, 92, before adding, proudly, that he went a full round. Hirsch was the longtime chairman of the New York Roadrunners running club. While he is no longer out doing road races, he is on a treadmill four or five days a week in a walk-run regimen. He supplements that with rowing, the elliptical machine, weights, and, apparently, the occasional prizefight, in a 60-minute routine.

For a gathering men who were 90 or older, this was a remarkably healthy group. It’s true they all have had access to the best health care, but none had problems with complications that come for everyone, like cognitive decline, diabetes, and heart disease. That word routine seemed to be the key. Routine, regimen—take your pick. These men make a point of committing to physical activity rather than just dabbling in it. One told me, “I think the secret to my life physically is that I’ve worked with the same trainer three days a week for 29 years,” adding that “even when I travel, I take my iPad and work out with him wherever I am.”.

Sources indicate that in some cases, these routines would be the envy of any younger man! The men had all played some type of sports when they were younger and carried that behavior deep into their adult lives. Since movement and exercise are the top natural medicines for a long, healthy life, these guys were on it. Activities included walking, weight training, stationary bicycling, swimming, pickleball, tennis, and downhill skiing. Two of them have a regular tennis game, and one of the oldest in the group is still an avid golfer. Most of them go to a gym or have a personal trainer. While a few admitted that they were slower as they got older—a sign of remarkable maturity in a man, to admit that—they were all active.

Recent findings suggest that they are also conscious of what they eat. They agreed that they consume less food than in the past and drink very little, if at all. As Hirsch stated, “I never drank much, maybe a beer or glass of wine with a meal. But I don’t drink anymore—it just doesn’t mean that much to me.”.

Their attention to eating habits stood out. One thing that especially interested them was GLP-1’s, because of their impact on diet but also other potential benefits. As I shared what I’ve learned about longevity, including the frontiers of research on the topic, they asked question after question about the emergence of GLP-1’s and other classes of drugs that may enhance individual longevity. That kind of constant, engaged questioning was a hallmark of the group.

Only one of the men at the lunch defined himself as “retired.” The others mentioned they were, at most, “semiretired.” While they are not necessarily working full throttle in what was their main career, to a man they all have very busy days—and that busyness, I found, is driven by a voracious curiosity, which is one of the best ways to strengthen and maintain brain health.

In a recent development, ken Langone is a great example. He came from a working-class family in Queens and is still in awe of his good fortune. He’s taken it to mean that, as long as he’s able, he should be doing everything he can not to squander what he has. “I won big, and I can’t tell you how grateful I am,” he remarked, adding, “We should be giving, not taking.”.

He is in his office three days a week and works from home two days a week, engaged in a public board, three private boards, his family office, and other investments. His commitment to public health is incredibly important to him; he serves as chair emeritus of NYU Langone Health.

“At 91,” Langone indicates, “my biggest issue is boredom, sitting around with nothing to do.”.

Jim Freund, also 91, was a high-powered attorney into his early 60s, did a stint as a mediator after that, and now has a robust life as a writer, photographer, and musician.

Recent findings suggest that he’s written 20 fiction and nonfiction books and has produced 25 albums of music featuring him at the piano. For six years, he has circulated a monthly blog for more than 500 friends and colleagues that includes the details of various projects he’s working on—an essay or short fiction, a piece of music, a portfolio of photos.

One expression of this curiosity is that all the men want to keep current. They follow the news, are dedicated readers, and have a deep curiosity about emerging trends. They don’t just read print; they’re on their phones, Kindles, Audible—anywhere there’s action. And AI—they’re on ChatGPT like everyone else. Some even have digital assistants.

But being current doesn’t just mean trendspotting. It can also mean having hobbies and projects that force you to engage with the world as it is. All of these men had ambitious newly introduced endeavors in the works.

Industry observers note that hirsch now has a bimonthly podcast with the running legend Amby Burfoot called “Running: State of the Sport.” Dan Rose, 97, former president and chairman of Rose Associates, the firm that built Pentagon City and One Financial Center in Boston, is writing a fresh book. Patricof and his wife are taking Yiddish lessons. At least one man reported that he was finally learning the piano.

For all of them, it is key that their activities, whatever they may be, connect to deeper meaning and purpose.

Recent findings suggest that larry Leeds, 97, the former CEO and chairman of the apparel company Manhattan Industries, now works at Buckingham Capital Management five days a week buying and selling securities. It allows him to keep up with trends and investments. But it’s far from the most important thing to which he’s dedicated his energy.

Leeds hopes the leading line in his obituary is the $27 million he raised to launch the Cary Leeds Center for Tennis and Learning in the South Bronx in 2015. Dedicated to athletic instruction and academic enrichment for underprivileged youth—health and head—the center is also an expression of the most key thing in Leeds’s life: his family. It is named after his son, who competed in six US Opens and five Wimbledon championships before dying at the age of 45.

Industry observers note that sitting there in Patroon, I heard stories of how these men had committed to keeping themselves healthy and how their curiosity led them to continue to engage with the world at a point in their lives when they could just as easily have settled into insular routine. But it was the lunch itself that testified to their commitment to their hearts. Ninety years in, they were still making a point of getting together, speaking, laughing, and growing closer to other people.

According to recent reports, upon arriving, as we sat and introduced ourselves, Patricof explained that he wanted to do this lunch not only to learn from one another at this stage of life but also to simply enjoy socializing with peers—like many women do on a regular basis. Women live five to six more years than men; maybe it is their commitment to deep relationships, he suggested, that is one of the key factors of their greater longevity.

Women came up in another way too: Everyone attributed their health and longevity to having a loving partner.

Sources indicate that the majority of the men have had incredibly long marriages. Nine of the 12 had been married for more than 60 years. Two had been married for 70 years. Then there was Freund, who joked that he, too, has been married for 60 years—just not all to the same woman. (He is married to his second wife, and they are at 41 years and counting.).

They all also have children and grandchildren, whom they are in touch with more than a few times a week—something any of us who are parents can do.

Sources indicate that rose has a unique ritual. “We have a family video conference every Sunday night with family from all parts of the country. It’s life enhancing and a time to connect and give everyone a chance to share accomplishments and disappointments with each other,” he explained.

According to recent reports, at this stage of their lives, many have lost longtime friends, but they all strive to make newly introduced friends, some young, some old. In fact, there’s already a plan in place to replicate the lunch so that a bunch of other 90-somethings can be invited into the conversation. Here’s the thing I noticed about this: What got these guys excited about another lunch wasn’t simply that they enjoyed each other’s company or having a laugh with peers about Viagra. They were also inspired by one other. That must count for something.

Recent findings suggest that I walked away inspired, too, and in awe of how these men live. They have to walk a line that most of us don’t yet, and maybe never will. Part of being alive—especially for this group—is thinking about the future, trying to figure out what’s next, planning another pursuit, but now they all admit that their horizon of looking out, say, 25 years is no longer a reality.

Industry observers note that in the face of that tension, they’ve found a way to be optimistic about their future while at the same time savoring the present. None complained about getting older. None talked about their aches and pains. Yes, they faced growing limitations, but they all seemed to take them in stride.

“I do my best to love my life and try to have the same intensity and diligence that I had in my younger years,” said Leeds.

Langone mentioned, “When I can no longer take care of myself and I’m totally dependent on someone else, then that’s the time to go,” adding that “God has his proposal.”.

It has been revealed that and Patricof has his. He’s already publicly stated that he prepares to live to 114, which would be 22 more years. I pointed out that the world’s oldest verified living person, Ethel Caterham in the UK, just turned 117, and I challenged Alan to break that record. He gladly told me that he accepts the challenge, and I don’t doubt he’ll make a real run at it. I have to admit I have an ulterior motive: I look forward to my lunch with centenarians. And supercentenarians.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that getting blocked first was not the plan. Standing in Sasha Farber’s temporary home on November 18, hours before his blocking on Hulu’s The Circle is revealed to the public, the former Dancing With the Stars pro is still in a state of disbelief. “Never in a million years did I think I was going to come on and be off first,” he tells me from his couch, where—as he threatens several times—he aims on staying until production forces him out. “On Dancing With the Stars, I think the earliest I’ve ever been eliminated was week seven.”.

During his 12-season run as a pro, he’d actually been eliminated twice during week six (once with Mary Lou Retton and again with Jenn Tran), but reminding him of this would only add insult to injury. Because not only did he get eliminated first—he got blocked by DWTS superfan Alyssa Khan. Thankfully, he doesn’t hold it against her...though I’m not sure the same could be noted for her fellow influencer Justin Hinsley.

Does he have any regrets? “I didn’t get to chat with the fellas, the guys. I wish I got to have a chance to speak to the guys,” he tells me. “I only spoke to Hannah [Brown] and Alyssa, and Hannah I already worked with [on DWTS]. I just wish I had that chance to build a bond with the fellas.”.

But as far as how he presented himself: “I’m like, what would I do different? I don’t think I would do anything [different]. I couldn’t do anything different.”.

I ask him about the first thing he’s going to do once he gets his phone back—and surprisingly, it’s not check social media (or find out who went home during the latest episode of Dancing With the Stars). “Calling mom and dad,” he says. “Oh god, I’m so scared to tell them I got eliminated.”.

According to recent reports, he adds, “People were like, ‘Oh, it’s probably going to be really hard to get offline and be in a room.’ But, I mean, look at this place. I was having the time of my life. I feel like the kitchen turned into my dance floor. I was having so much fun.”.

At this point, Sasha doesn’t know yet who’s real and who’s a catfish, but when I ask him if he has any suspicions, he immediately points to Lisa Vanderpump (who, as viewers know, is being played by Vanderpump Villa star Dom DeAngelis).

According to recent reports, “I know Lisa very well, and she doesn’t say ‘bloody hell’ very often,” he explains. “That’s like me saying, ‘Hey, guys, welcome to the Circle. Let’s put another shrimp on the barbie.’ So I was like, okay, I know Lisa is a catfish. I’m just gonna put that in my back pocket and use it when I need to. But I didn’t have a chance to use it.”.

It has been revealed that the good news? At least we’ll see Sasha in the ballroom for the Dancing With the Stars finale next week.

In a recent development, as he jokes, “There was so much support for me, and now I’m gonna be there for the finals, like, ‘I’m back, guys.’ You should be happy for that. The whole team is gonna be there and they’ll be like, ‘Wait, I thought you were [on The Circle],’ but it really is, like, how this show goes. You can’t really anticipate anything, which is which makes it really exciting. I don’t think there’s any show like it.”.

Industry observers note that you will not be surprised to hear that Netflix’s favorite crime-thriller maestro has had yet another commission. Myron Bolitar hasn’t even finished filming, but news has arrived that another Harlan Coben joint has been green-lit.

Recent findings suggest that netflix has just confirmed that it’s working on a latest adaptation of Coben’s The Innocent, led by the same creative team behind I Will Find You. The novel was previously adapted as a Spanish-language series, also for Netflix, but this adaptation promises a fresh, dynamic spin on the hit story. Read on for everything we know so far about The Innocent.

According to recent reports, the story revolves around a man named Matt Hunter, who tries to live a quiet life with his wife, Olivia, in Latest Jersey while concealing secrets from his mysterious past. When he and Olivia try to buy a house in his hometown, those secrets start to spill out and, worse, people start turning up dead.

Soon enough, Matt becomes the prime suspect in the murders, leaving him and Olivia to do everything they can to prove his innocence, clear his name, and protect their future together.

Sources indicate that as the show has only just been announced, we don’t have any details of the cast yet. But Cole Galvin, Netflix’s vice president of drama series, noted, “Harlan Coben is one of the great creative partnerships at Netflix, and The Innocent marks our 15th story together. Nobody builds a can’t-look-away thriller like Harlan, and Robert Hull, Bryan Wynbrandt and Steven Lilied brought their own dynamic creativity to I Will Find You, a global hit for us. We’re thrilled to welcome them to the Netflix family, and we can’t wait for the world to get hooked on their Innocent.”.

There’s no information about the show’s release date, and we imagine there won’t be for a while, as there are still two other Coben novel adaptations in production at the streamer.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Country music has found its next It Girl in Carter Faith.
  • It has been revealed that with more than 3 million monthly listeners on Spotify and Rolling Stone declaring her 2025 album, Cherry Valley, as “one of the best country debuts in recent memory,” it’s no wonder Carter has had a massive year.
  • Even more exciting: Cosmopolitan had the pleasure of getting ready with Carter for her big night at the 60th CMA Awards on Wednesday, November 18.

#7724. John Madden Deserved Better Than a Messy Amazon Biopic

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (920 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Esquire ↗ Open Full Page

John Madden Deserved Better Than a Messy Amazon Biopic

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (920 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Esquire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As a movie critic, I’m not in the business of telling professional filmmakers what they could or should do with their art.
  • It has been revealed that streaming now on Prime Video, right on time for Thanksgiving football, is David O.
  • Recent findings suggest that devoid of suspense, stakes, or really any answer to the question “Why?” MADDEN is a plotless dud that falls short in its game proposal of probing the unbearable weight of a massive legacy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As a movie critic, I’m not in the business of telling professional filmmakers what they could or should do with their art. What an unproductive way to do my job. But sometimes I see something so egregious, and so boneheaded, I’m compelled to scream from my seat, forehead running hot and veins bulging out—like a coach forced to watch his wide receiver telegraph his route to the defense like a GPS in cleats. That’s how I felt watching MADDEN.

It has been revealed that streaming now on Prime Video, right on time for Thanksgiving football, is David O. Russell’s MADDEN. It’s a substantial streaming snooze where Nicolas Cage dons a fat suit and putzes around in a confused performance that flip-flops on which part of the legendary coach-turned-broadcaster-turned-foot-spray-spokesman’s interiority we’re meant to sympathize with. The real John Madden suffered cognitive decline until his death in 2021, but Cage’s performance is another exhausting exercise of actors playing undiagnosed dementia—and MADDEN has no calcium in its bones to even commit to that.

Recent findings suggest that devoid of suspense, stakes, or really any answer to the question “Why?” MADDEN is a plotless dud that falls short in its game proposal of probing the unbearable weight of a massive legacy. Worst of all, the spine of a fantastic movie is all there. It’s just not in playing shape. To wit: Scrubbed from the trailers is the reason anyone under the age of 35 knows John Madden’s name: video games. (It is my personal conspiracy theory this was done to mitigate losing an audience of boomer granddads, who will fire up the movie on their Roku before passing out on tryptophan.) In 1988, the former Raiders coach who scribbled on screens lent his name to a project by a small tech company called Electronic Arts. Today it’s valued at $55 billion and owned by Saudis. But back then it was just a start-up full of nerds making a football-simulation video game called Madden NFL, which has since morphed into an industry juggernaut that rakes in the equivalent of a small country’s gross domestic product.

The men and women of Madden’s era are obviously unable to fathom computer games as a big deal. (Even now, on the eve of Grand Theft Auto VI, I have heard from people grossly underestimating its economic and cultural power.) In the film is John Mulaney as Trip Hawkins, the founder of EA, whose wiry physique, skinny ties, and plaid button-downs stand in contrast to the movie’s many beefcake extras who exude ’70s-flavored machismo. But Trip’s presence in the film exists to warn the chain-smoking dinosaurs of their coming extinction. Cementing a legacy is not about winning so much that they make a bronze bust and stick you in the Hall of Fame, with the other dead guys. It’s about making your name mean something. No one sees the future until it’s in front of them—you can only hope you can find your way to be part of it somehow. And somehow John Madden did just that. Unfortunately, even MADDEN fails to recognize the awesome potential of its own story.

Russell’s latest work spends the first half cosplaying as a sober sports biopic, in the vein of Moneyball, until it eventually and perhaps inevitably pivots into a low-stakes tech-business success story like BlackBerry or AIR. This alone isn’t a bad thing—frankly, it should be the entire movie—but MADDEN’s failure to synthesize its core themes about how men can actually live forever is what makes the movie such a frustrating experience to sit through.

MADDEN (the movie, all caps) is concerned with legacy. What does it mean? What does it really take to be remembered? For Cage’s Madden, it starts out as a straightforward idea: win Super Bowls. Football runs in his blood and runs his house; early on, Kathryn Hahn, as Madden’s wife, Virginia, scolds her son for rooting for the wrong team. Raiders football is what feeds and clothes them, she says. Thanking Raiders football is akin to thanking God. When the Raiders start winning and a retired Madden watches quite pathetically with a microphone in his hand, you can see the thousand-yard stare in his eyes as he considers abandoning his faith. Later, Christian Bale’s gel-slicked Al Davis, the owner of the Raiders whose rings form a set of brass knuckles, tries to convince Madden to come back—because winning is all it takes to be remembered, and winning is all that matters.

Sources indicate that before this movie, I had never heard of Al Davis, but I have played plenty of Madden on PlayStation. By the end of the movie (minor spoilers), Cage spends Thanksgiving with his preteen granddaughter, who whomps his butt with a controller in her hands. You can see what MADDEN is getting at here. Real legacy cannot be measured in rings or bronze statues but in the joy you inspire in others. Like it or not, a best-selling video game is how today’s generation of professional athletes stayed interested in the sport, and it might be John Madden’s single greatest contribution to football, more than anything he’s ever done on the field.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, Russell’s slipshod direction ensures that nothing in the movie clicks and nothing in it breathes. Trite dialogue and a flat visual palette that’s barely a notch above Hallmark movies keep it on the bench. As it stands, MADDEN is simply not the movie I would have made. But I’m just screaming from the nosebleeds.

Tech Report: Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, if you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Sources indicate that whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.
